title: Vulnerability scan, SAST or penetration test: which do you need in 2026?
summary: SAST reads code, scanners check known issues, a pentest proves what an attacker can exploit. See which one you need in 2026, with OWASP and NIST sources.
body_markdown:
Short answer: run SAST and vulnerability scans all the time, and add a penetration test whenever someone needs proof of what an attacker can actually do. SAST reads your code for insecure patterns. A vulnerability scanner checks running systems for known issues. Only a penetration test tries to exploit what it finds and shows you the result.[CodeAnt AI](https://www.codeant.ai/) fits teams that want both sides in one platform:[code security](https://www.codeant.ai/code-security) (SAST, SCA, secrets and IaC) plus an[AI pentest](https://www.codeant.ai/pentesting) that delivers a report mapped to SOC 2 and ISO 27001 within 48 hours, with a researcher checking every critical finding.


CodeAnt AI has run 12,000 pentests and is trusted by more than 1,000 companies, including Fortune 500 companies like NRG, cybersecurity leaders like Commvault, and fast-growing companies like 11x and Sanas.


The rest of this guide explains what each test finds, where each one stops, and which you need for your situation.


## What Does Each Test Actually Find?


### SAST: insecure patterns in your code


[OWASP's DevSecOps Guideline](https://owasp.github.io/DevSecOpsGuideline/2-Process/2-3-Build/2-3-1-Static-Analysis/2-3-1-1-Static-Application-Security-Testing/) describes static application security testing as analysis of source code, bytecode or binaries without executing it. It runs in the IDE, at pre-commit and in CI, and it points to the vulnerable line, which makes it the cheapest place to catch a bug. OWASP is equally clear about its limits: SAST cannot see runtime or environment context, it flags safe code as vulnerable, and it can miss flaws that only appear at runtime, such as logic bugs and authentication issues that depend on data state.


### Vulnerability scanning: known issues on running systems


A vulnerability scanner probes your live hosts, apps and APIs and matches what it sees against databases of known vulnerabilities and misconfigurations. DAST is the application flavor of the same idea (see[SAST vs DAST](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/sast-vs-dast) ).[NIST SP 800-115](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-115.pdf) (section 4.3) notes that application scanners typically have high false positive rates, share the false negatives of every signature-based tool, and cannot detect vulnerabilities that only appear when several weaknesses are combined. NIST's own answer to that gap is penetration testing.


### Penetration testing: proof of what an attacker can do


[NIST SP 800-115](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-115.pdf) (section 5.2) defines penetration testing as security testing in which assessors mimic real-world attacks to find ways around your security features, usually by combining vulnerabilities to gain more access than any single flaw allows. The[OWASP Web Security Testing Guide](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/2-Introduction/) puts the trade plainly: tools excel at known, signature-based vulnerabilities but do not understand business logic or context, so the answer is to layer human-grade testing on top of tooling, not to pick one.

## Is Snyk or a SAST Tool Enough, or Do You Need a Penetration Test?


SAST is enough to keep insecure code out of your main branch. It is not enough to tell you, a customer or an auditor what an attacker can reach in the deployed product. Add a penetration test when any of these are true:


-


You have more than one user role or tenant, so broken authorization (one user reading another user's data) is possible. SAST sees each function, not the permissions between them.


-


Your API has multi-step workflows such as checkout, refunds or invitations, where abuse lives in the sequence of calls rather than in one line of code.


-


A customer security review, an investor or a framework asks for a penetration test report. A SAST export does not answer that question.


-


You changed authentication, billing, permissions or infrastructure since the last test.


-


New APIs and subdomains appear faster than your team tracks them, so the code you scan is not the full surface an attacker sees.


## Why Do Scanner Findings Stall Before Anyone Fixes Them?


Security leads we speak with describe the same loop. The scanner marks something critical, a developer asks why it is critical and how it could be exploited, and without steps to reproduce, the ticket waits. The question they bring to a pentest is direct: what can an outsider exploit today and walk out with data? Show me that first.


Teams that already gate pull requests on SAST, SCA and[secret scanning](https://www.codeant.ai/secret-scanning) still buy a pentest. Often it is a once-a-year compliance test of a limited set of APIs, and the worry is everything that ships between tests, such as a new endpoint without authorization that nobody on the security team knew existed. That is the gap a scan cannot close and a point-in-time test closes only once a year.

## Won't a Pentest Just Repeat What My Scanners Already Found?


A good one starts there and goes further.[NIST SP 800-115](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-115.pdf) notes that penetration testing usually relies on port and service identification and vulnerability scanning to find targets, then tries to exploit them and combine weaknesses. What you should get back is not the scanner list again but a short list of findings that are proven exploitable, with the request and response that proves each one and the fix. If a pentest report reads like a scanner export, ask the vendor how much authenticated testing was done and how each finding was verified.


## We Already Run DAST in CI. Is That a Pentest?


No. DAST vendors say so themselves: StackHawk states that DAST cannot fully replace penetration testing. DAST is a fast runtime check on every build; a pentest is an attempt to break the application the way an attacker would, including logic and permission flaws a scanner does not reason about.
